title: Synthetic Data Generation
summary: Analyze how recursive synthetic training can degrade tail coverage and diversity over generations.

blocks.md:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Analyze how recursive synthetic training can degrade tail coverage and diversity over generations
- Analyze knowledge distillation as a data-synthesis lever by locating its storage and input-pipeline cost
- Analyze domain gap challenges and justify synthetic-to-real mixing ratios
- Evaluate the misconception that advanced generative models eliminate domain shift

blocks.source: Vol I, Data Selection, § Synthetic Data Generation
blocks.md: Real-world data collection encounters physical and legal boundaries: autonomous fleets cannot safely crash vehicles to acquire catastrophic collision trajectories, healthcare systems cannot transmit protected patient telemetry across institutional firewalls, and edge products must handle acoustic environments before any deployed fleet exists to record them. When the source corpus contains few or none of the cases deployment will face, neither static pruning nor dynamic selection can extract signal that is not there.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Data augmentation
- Generative synthesis
- Bridging the domain gap
- Knowledge distillation

Pay attention to: Model collapse; Offline distillation targets as a data cost; Synthetic-real mixing and the domain gap; Limits of generated data.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Why is training exclusively on \$100\% synthetic data from a simulation engine often suboptimal for real-world deployment, and how does synthetic-to-real data mixing bridge this gap?
blocks.md: Simulation engines have an inherent domain gap ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{synth}} \ne \mathcal{D}_{\text{real}}$) caused by simplified physics, missing sensor artifacts, and unmodeled environmental noise. Mixing synthetic data with a curated set of real-world examples anchors the model to real feature distributions while using synthetic samples to expand volume, cover edge cases, and balance rare classes.

questions.q: What causes the phenomenon of 'model collapse' when generative models are trained recursively on synthetic data generated by earlier model iterations?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D. The section's model-collapse mechanism is recursive tail erosion: generated data underrepresents rare but important patterns, and retraining on later synthetic generations compounds those omissions and errors. High-probability modes dominating the sample stream is part of that story, but it does not prove universal collapse under every sampling regime. The other choices are execution problems, not the chapter's statistical mechanism.
questions.hint: Think about: analyze how recursive synthetic training can degrade tail coverage and diversity over generations.
options: GPU memory fragmentation caused by variable-length synthetic sequences during distributed training
Overfitting to floating-point rounding errors during fp16 mixed-precision matrix multiplication
A failure of the I/O storage subsystem to deliver synthetic batches at line rate
Systematic underrepresentation and erosion of tail patterns across generations, so recursive retraining compounds missing or distorted rare cases

questions.q: A team distills a ResNet-50 student on ImageNet and chooses offline distillation, precomputing the teacher's FP32 logits for every training image instead of keeping the teacher in accelerator memory. Which cost does this choice move onto the data path?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. Offline distillation stores one logit per class for every sample, so the per-sample label grows from a single integer index to four bytes per class, an expansion of more than three orders of magnitude for ImageNet's thousand classes, and every epoch reads it back through the input pipeline. Teacher residency and the reduced student batch size are the costs of online distillation, which this choice avoids. Soft targets do not force a lower learning rate, and the teacher pass runs once during precomputation rather than once per epoch.
questions.hint: Think about: analyze knowledge distillation as a data-synthesis lever by locating its storage and input-pipeline cost.
options: Every epoch must read per-class logit vectors in place of single integer labels, multiplying the label bytes the storage tier and input pipeline must deliver
Every training step must run a teacher forward pass beside the student, restricting the student's per-accelerator batch size
The student must be trained with a lower learning rate, because soft targets produce larger gradients than one-hot labels
The teacher must be retrained once per student epoch, so preparation cost grows linearly with the number of epochs

questions.q: Using a high-capacity diffusion model or state-of-the-art LLM to generate synthetic training data guarantees that the resulting training set will be completely free of distribution shift relative to the real deployment environment.
questions.explanation: False. Generator quality does not eliminate domain gap. Synthetic generators can amplify subtle distribution shifts, introduce generator-specific artifacts, and omit edge cases present in real-world deployment environments, requiring domain validation against real ground truth.
questions.hint: Think about: evaluate the misconception that advanced generative models eliminate domain shift.
